results.question: What does the book say about making your own chroma keyer?
results.answer:
The book describes two DIY approaches — an HSV-based keyer built from a color curve node, and a 3D RGB color-cube variant — then promptly warns that a home-built chroma keyer is more trouble than it's worth.

## How to build it

The recipe in Section 2.2.2 mirrors the homemade luma keyer from Section 2.1.3: start with an operation that converts the RGB image to HSV, then pipe the HSV image into a color curve node [S1][S17]. The trick is that the curves now carry different data than they do for RGB — the RED curve holds Hue, the GREEN curve holds Saturation, and the BLUE curve holds Value (brightness) — so you adjust all three to include or exclude the hue, saturation, and value ranges of the target object [S1].

That approach mirrors how a commercial chroma keyer works internally. The book explains that a keyer converts RGB to HSV/HSL precisely because saturation is not an RGB attribute, then sets a starting pixel value as the "center" of the key and defines separate Hue, Saturation, and Value ranges around it: pixels inside go to white, outside go to black, and per-channel tolerances are what produce a soft-edged key instead of a sharp one [S14]. A simple keyer just picks a color/hue range and declares those pixels background; a good one also lets you constrain saturation and luminance [S3].

The second, more interesting path is a three-dimensional color keyer built on the RGB color cube rather than HSV — a grossly simplified version of Primatte's operating principles that keys any arbitrary color [S8]. The book gives an equation where R1G1B1 is the normalized center color you want to isolate and R2G2B2 is the normalized value of each pixel, which you can enter into a math node or any expression format your software supports [S13]. One caveat: the retrieved text references this equation but doesn't actually reproduce it, so its exact form would need to come from the printed section.

## The book's caveats

The practical verdict is blunt. Unlike the luma keyer, where cleverness can bring real improvements, the homemade chroma keyer "will probably be more hassle than its worth" — you might build one once to test your mettle, but an off-the-shelf chroma keyer is hard to improve upon [S2]. Chroma keys are more discriminating than luma keys because they consider both chrominance and luminance, but they carry their own limitations and liabilities, which the section explores along with workarounds [S15]. The book also notes that keying in general is fundamentally a "clever cheat" that merely appears to work well under most circumstances — so don't be surprised when things go wrong [S18]. If you want to practice, it points to a downloadable test image, "Chroma key Target.tif," designed for pulling keys on various parts of a colorful picture [S5].

results.question: What does the book say about nonsquare pixels?
results.answer:
The book treats nonsquare pixels as a display-format property, not a defect: a pixel whose width and height are not equal, shaped as a rectangle rather than a square, with that width-to-height relationship expressed as a **pixel aspect ratio** (PAR) [S1][S3]. Square pixels have a PAR of 1:1, as on a properly adjusted computer monitor [S1].

## Why they exist

Nonsquare pixels appear whenever the aspect ratio of the displayed image differs from the original digital image, which happens in film and video formats [S2]. Systems that apply a temporary "unsqueeze" to display such images are said to handle nonsquare pixels — but the pixels on your monitor still look properly proportioned; only the display is resized geometrically, and the underlying image data is never modified [S4]. In film, the same idea is called **squeezed** or **anamorphic** formatting (an art-world term for a distorted image that can be restored), and the book uses Cinemascope's dramatic 2:1 squeeze as its running example [S5][S7].

## Technical implications

Pixel aspect ratio must not be confused with the image's overall aspect ratio — they can be completely different numbers [S13]. For NTSC analog video the book cites a PAR of 10:11 (pixels slightly taller than wide), meaning a perfectly round circle sent straight to video renders as an ellipse stretched 11/10ths vertically; depending on your setup you may need to scale manually or rely on an automated step [S13]. In compositing, rotating a squeezed element while it's still compressed produces visible distortion — the correct workflow is to unsqueeze, rotate, then re-squeeze along the x-axis, and even a 5° rotation leaves subtle errors, so anything working with nonsquare pixels warrants double-checking [S8].

## Formats cited

| Format | Resolution | Pixels | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| NTSC analog video | — | 10:11 PAR | Slightly taller than wide [S13] |
| NTSC-DV SD video | 720 × 480 | Rectangular | SD uses nonsquare pixels [S9] |
| PAL-DV SD video | 720 × 576 | Rectangular | SD uses nonsquare pixels [S9] |
| ATSC (one spec, rarely used) | 704 × 480 | 10:11 PAR | Produces 4:3 image [S11] |
| DTV / HD / computer graphics | 1920 × 1080, 640 × 480 | Square | 16:9 and 4:3 by design [S11][S9] |

The takeaway is that square pixels are the default for HD, graphics software, and monitors, while nonsquare pixels mainly belong to standard-definition video and anamorphic film workflows — and any compositing done in that world has to account for the squeeze before transforming or delivering [S9][S11][S7].

results.question: What does the book say about miscellaneous drawing tips?
results.answer:
The book's miscellaneous tips cluster around three recurring jobs: keeping drawings readable at a glance, keeping poses lively instead of stiff, and a set of process habits and specialty techniques for hard cases.

## Read at a glance

Draw bold — grease pencil, marker, or 2B pencil, never a hard pencil — so the drawing reads from across the room, and number your drawings [S2]. A drawing should survive the "blacken-in" test: if you fill in the shapes you can still read what's happening, decoration stays inside the main outline, and the outlines themselves are interesting — that keeps the drawing from getting busy [S1][S22]. On the storytelling side, draw attention to one idea at a time, "just like when speaking," and make sure the drawing says what you think it's saying [S7].

## Poses that move

Avoid symmetry — it's boring and makes figures look cut out; use angles, dynamic asymmetry, and play straight lines against curves instead [S6][S3]. Draw borders so you have to compose to them, use straight-line symbols for stretches and bent lines for squashes, and watch body landmarks where bones reach the surface, like hipbones and ribs [S6]. Feel the pose kinetically in your own body: a person is always "doing" something, so express the purpose and the emotion, highlight the important idea, and subordinate all else — while avoiding tricky camera angles that just make the drawing ambiguous [S6]. Don't get too clever, and when drawing eyes, darken the pupils [S3][S6].

## Process habits and special techniques

Learning to draw splits into two parts — technique (perspective, anatomy, force, shape) and honest observation — and the skill is diagnosing which side you're falling short on: a generic drawing means look more, while a specific-but-flat, dead, poorly designed one means apply technique [S5]. Always start with a rough sketch to clarify the image of the completed drawing and grasp the appearance/state of what you'll draw [S9]. Don't be afraid to redraw or cut out and rework parts that don't work; keep one idea per sketch and have something to say rather than doodling [S3]. One worked example is a jab-speed drawing where the artist drew the punched figure first to sell the impact, then made the puncher look even faster by comparison [S9]; another is a two-student exercise (one starts the drawing, another finishes it under a time restriction) that can yield one long continuous idea, with force sweeping through the pose from hip to foot, over the back, into the deltoid, and down to the wrist [S8].

**Drybrush** should be used very sparingly, only when drawings are so widely spaced the eye struggles to connect them — well-spaced drawings with well-anticipated fast action need no help [S4]; speed lines and motion blur generally illustrate the optical blur of an object moving too fast to see clearly, a device with roots in early newspaper cartoons [S21]. On **contour lines**, the book is philosophical: the lines in an average illustration don't exist in reality, they're only a means of defining space, and since perception changes with lighting, contour can sometimes get in the way — so master traditional line drawing first, then move into light-and-dark masses (chiaroscuro, "the line that never existed anyway") [S11][S14][S23]. Finally, **multiple moments**: drawing several moments of the same subject is more telling than a single drawing, reveals personality through action, and is a great exercise for proportion and volume — a good excuse for VCR/DVD reference [S10][S25].

results.question: What does the book say about transcoding versus color rerendering?
results.answer:
The book draws the line at the viewing environment: **transcoding** is a simple colorimetric conversion between displays that are essentially equivalent to view, while **color rerendering** is needed when the displays (or their viewing conditions) differ so much that appearance itself must be recomputed.

| | Transcoding | Color rerendering |
|---|---|---|
| When used | Displays match in black level, white luminance, viewing conditions, and gamma; only primaries differ [S2] | Displays' contrast, white levels, or viewing conditions are grossly dissimilar [S1] |
| Process | Linearize display 1's RGB → convert to CIE XYZ → convert to display 2's RGB → reimpose encoding gamma [S2] | Undo any color rendering done for display 1, yielding non-color-rendered CIE XYZ, then color render those values for display 2 [S1] |
| What it preserves | The colorimetry of the image | The appearance of the image under different viewing conditions |

The key term is **color rendering**: the transformation of an image to account for differences in the viewing environment, as opposed to a purely numerical re-encoding [S4]. The canonical example in the book is a digital still camera producing JPEGs, which color renders the capture to bridge the gap between a subject in bright desert sunlight and the reproduction on an office monitor whose peak white is hundreds of times dimmer [S4].

This distinction drives real workflow decisions in post-production. With camera raw, the encoded viewing environment is implicitly the original scene itself, so color rendering must be done downstream — and it is far easier for the visual effects team to *do* the rendering than to *undo* rendering a manufacturer baked into a non-raw format [S6]. The same logic appears in the ACES pipeline: the RRT provides a standard rendering for dark-surround theatrical viewing [S3], and the ODT then adapts that rendered data to each display device, with gamut mapping still required for low-gamut targets like HDTV [S9].

results.question: What does the book say about FACE OFF?
results.answer:
The corpus answers "face off" in two ways, both from its fight-choreography material — neither of them the 1997 John Woo film, which the evidence does not discuss.

**The confrontation beat** — "They square off and face each other in fighting stances" [S6] and "Fighter A meets Fighter B in the center of the ring" [S8] describe the classic standoff moment that sets up a fight: the two opponents face each other in their stances, establishing opposition and space before any action begins. This is the standard pre-fight framing used in choreographed scenes.

**The stunt-fall term** — in the book's glossary of fighting and fight-choreography terminology, "face-off" is defined as "a fall that starts face-first, but where you tuck and rotate last-minute to land on your back" [S1][S16]. It's a safety technique: the performer commits to a face-first drop but converts it mid-air into a controlled back landing.

So in cinema context, "face off" names both the dramatic standoff between fighters and a specific protected fall for stunt performers. If you meant the film *Face/Off* (John Woo, 1997), that movie isn't covered in the retrieved material.

results.question: What does the book say about affect, fatigue, and injury are control states?
results.answer:
The book’s heading is explicit: affect, fatigue, and injury are control states — they must change later action selection and execution, and they are not adjectives appended after choreography is chosen [S23]. In other words, they are upstream parameters the system consumes when picking and running movement, not labels stuck onto an already-designed scene.

| State | What it tracks | How it changes execution | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Affect | Appraisal of the situation (goal congruence, controllability, certainty) plus valence/arousal/dominance | Narrows attention toward the exit lane, makes recovery urgent but less clean, raises risk tolerance for one recovery attempt | [S1] |
| Injury | Mechanical capacity losses and compensations (pain, severity, load acceptance, flexion, push-off) | Favors the healthy leg, shortens the injured leg's stance, increases trunk lean during emergency recovery | [S2] |
| Fatigue | Global exertion (RPE, breath cycle, recovery rate) and local capacity per limb | Increases step-width variability, lengthens stabilization after hard redirection, shifts work to the shoulder/leg that still has capacity | [S3] |

**Affect** is framed as an appraisal update: a trigger (e.g., expected interception fails, north lane opens) produces posterior scores — negative valence, higher arousal, lower dominance — with explicit behavioral consequences attached [S1]. The book warns against compiling emotions into deterministic motion, e.g., “anger = always faster” or “fear = always retreat”; kinematic-emotion links are population-level at best, with character, culture, injury, and tactical intent remaining moderators [S9].

**Injury** is specified as an object with mechanical consequences and compensations, and it carries an explicit uncertainty tag: the source is dramatic annotation rather than clinical measurement, with confidence only 0.70 [S2]. Relatedly, the book treats pain as something that alters the voice and breath — injuries near the body's center lower pitch, peripheral injuries raise it, and adrenaline can mask injury severity in the moment [S6]. In fight scenes specifically, expressing pain is about control: deliberate martial intent versus being moved against one's will versus reflexive reactions like flinch, squirm, or spasm [S24].

**Fatigue** is modeled as both a global and a local capacity state, with coordination-level effects on how movement degrades [S3], and the book proposes a compiler-state update equation: f(t+Δt) = clamp(f(t) + work + impact − recovery, 0, 1), where f is fatigue (not remaining capacity) and the work/impact/recovery terms must be calibrated rather than inferred from prose [S4].

The three overlap in that they all modulate the same downstream machinery, and they plausibly interact — an urgent affective state raises risk tolerance for a recovery attempt while an injured, fatigued left leg lowers what that attempt can ask of the limb. One caveat: the retrieved material gives the full specification for fatigue, but the corpus does not contain a broader passage developing fatigue's control-state role beyond this spec block and equation. Also worth distinguishing: these control states are a different layer from the six Laban effort states (mobile, stable, remote, rhythm, dream, awake), which describe combinations of effort factors in the movement vocabulary itself rather than the physiological/affective modulators acting on it [S5][S8][S10].

results.question: What does the book say about movement of an object with a background?
results.answer:
The book treats an object's movement as something that only becomes visible in relation to the frame line and to the background behind it — so the background is not scenery but the reference system against which movement is read [S9][S12]. It frames this in two complementary ways: movement seen against a stationary scene (relative movement) and movement read onto a scene from other moving elements (induced movement).

## How the background reveals movement

**Relative movement** is the standard case: one object's motion is gauged by its changing position against a second, stationary object and the frame [S4][S23]. But the book also describes **induced movement**, where a moving object transfers its apparent motion to a nearby stationary object, making the stationary one seem to move [S2]. Its central example is a car being followed by a panning camera in a forest: the car stays fixed in the frame, yet the trees stream past in the opposite direction, generating apparent movement that the viewer transfers to the car. The trees reveal the car is moving even though it has no relative movement against the frame [S10]. The strongest contrast to all this is **tableau staging** — a production in which object movement is minimized entirely, with interest carried by the stationary arrangement of objects [S3].

## Combining a moving object with a background

When a moving object is composited over a background, the book names three visual factors to weigh: the **direction of the track** the object creates, the **orientation of the background's linear motif** (its dominant lines), and the **contrast or affinity** between that track and the background pattern [S11]. Movement itself is categorized by direction, quality, scale, and speed, and every moving object generates a track — the path of its motion, of which there are actual and virtual types [S5]. Shot continuity matters across edits too: a movement begun in one shot should carry into the next, as in a straight-line move across the frame's lower quadrant followed by a curved move starting from where it ended [S7][S19].

## Camera movement, parallax, and compositing

**Match moving** keeps object and background coherent when the camera moves: because the background must move appropriately to the foreground, tracking data is extracted from the foreground image and applied to the background during compositing [S6][S21]. Layering moving objects also yields **motion parallax** — the variation in image travel between objects at different distances — which conveys their position and separation in depth [S8]. Lens choice amplifies these effects: a telephoto's reduced field of view combined with a circular tracking move around a static subject makes the background appear to revolve rapidly behind it [S18]. And for visual-effects extraction, the book notes that a motion-blurred object over a neutral background is easy to pull with a blurred rotoshape, while the same object over a detailed background is much harder — a soft-edged matte that includes the blur will also grab background detail [S1].

results.question: What does the book say about sound editing?
results.answer:
Sound editing, in this book, is the postproduction phase where all of the film's sound details get worked out: whatever production didn't capture is created afterward, and the result is described as even more elaborate and decision-heavy than the picture edit, because a wrong sound decision can so readily undermine the visuals [S1]. The editor's first task is to determine the narrative point of each scene and then surround that point with supporting sound — in *The Battle of Algiers*, for example, the narrative point is authenticity, and the sound must support that [S1][S8].

## Goals and principles

The rough sound edit pursues the same aims as the rough picture assembly — believable performances and a progressive sense of story — while dramatic emphasis and metaphor wait for the fine cut [S8]. Because viewers process sound more rapidly than images, believability is the sound edit's most urgent task: unbelievable sound undermines the visuals and loses the audience's involvement, so narrative clarity and believability are the primary goals, along with judging how much or how little dialogue a scene actually needs [S8][S9]. Whatever the scope, special care in building and mixing tracks applies across the board, from a two-track music video to a 62-track blockbuster; a well-populated, well-mixed track is what earns descriptors like "full," "rich," and "engrossing" [S10][S4].

## The process

Editing gathers or creates the audio assets: the editor and sound designers acquire additional files that augment — and sometimes replace — production-recorded sound, generating a new, often more realistic "reality" for the narrative [S4]. Once dialogue editing is done, the creative phase begins; the sound designer, whose role is likened to the director of photography's, oversees the individual tracks for dialogue, ambience, hard sound effects, and foley [S12]. Sound is manufactured in the name of believability: dialogue is looped or redubbed in a studio with the performer watching the projected performance, effects come from libraries or are recreated (a slap, a cricket, a footstep), music is built separately, and narration is often written at this stage to clarify the visuals [S14]. The book also catalogues the standard toolkit — foley and spot effects, wild sound and wild locations, room tone, presence tracks, sound logs — and expects the sound editor, at the end of the job, to shape the overall design and hand it to the director and the rerecording team as a guide for the mix [S7][S3][S6].

The mix is where the meaning of the sound is finally decided. Separating effects lets the mixer fade one out while fading another in for smooth transitions, while a continuous sound carried across two disparate visuals implies a link between them — so the mix can separate or connect shots, and can imply the passage or the continuity of time; a feature-film mix can run to 60 tracks [S15]. On the creative-manipulation side, the sound-design material in the collection covers pitch and speed manipulation, musique concrète, and effects built from everyday objects — cellophane crumpled for fire, salt and rice sprinkled on paper for rain and hail, and hands working soggy newspaper for footsteps in mud [S29][S32].

## A historical footnote

The book adds that sound originally inhibited editing: dialogue recorded on disc and early Movietone sound could not survive a cut without losing synchronization, so editing was confined to silent sequences until rerecording and multiple-camera setups became common [S13]. That history explains why the elaborate postproduction sound edit described above is now so central to a picture's success.

results.question: What does the book say about write radio sparely?
results.answer:
The book's central instruction is blunt: **write sparely** unless the concept genuinely demands a lot of words and fast action, because spare writing lets voice talent read slowly — "quietly. One word at a time" [S2][S16]. Sparse scripts are also safer under real production pressure: most radio spots are promotional and carry client tags that eat into the clock, so writing lean from the start leaves room for them [S1].

Several practical techniques come with that advice:

- **Time out mandatories first.** If a bank commercial must end with legal copy, write that material as sparely as possible and time it, then fit the rest of the spot into whatever time remains [S3].
- **Underwrite on purpose.** Overwriting is called the most common mistake in radio — "Be a genius. Underwrite" [S3].
- **Avoid fat scripts at the studio.** Showing up with an overlong script means editing under pressure and without client approval; even non-bare-bones ideas should be written sparely [S4].
- **Use silence like white space.** The book argues bare-bones executions leap out of the radio, and that silence holds remarkable power — "It is to radio what white space is to print," enlarging the idea it surrounds [S10].
- **Respect the :30's scale.** If a 60-second spot is a house, a :30 is a tent — a different animal, at roughly 60 words [S21].

The book also frames idea generation separately from script writing: come up with a lot of concepts and scribble each general thought on a Post-it Note rather than drafting full scripts [S5]. The through-line is that underwriting protects pacing, leaves room for required material, and lets the idea breathe in a medium where a spot exists only while it's playing [S8].
